1.definition: A Ghurid Turkic mamluk commander who held Ghazni after Muhammad of Ghor’s 1206 assassination and contested Aibak’s claim to the Indian Ghurid provinces. Iltutmish defeated him, ending his bid for the fragmenting Ghurid inheritance.

A Ghurid Turkic mamluk commander who controlled Sindh and Multan and contested the early Sultanate’s authority after 1206. Iltutmish defeated him in 1228, consolidating the Indian Ghurid territories under Delhi.

The fifth Mughal emperor (ruled 1628–1658), who built the modern Old Delhi — Shahjahanabad — at the northern end of the cluster of Sultanate cities in 1648, and built the Taj Mahal at Agra. His Shahjahanabad is the seventh of the "seven cities of Delhi."
The walled city the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan built in 1648 at the northern end of the Delhi cluster — modern Old Delhi, the last of the "seven cities of Delhi" that began with Aibak’s Mehrauli.
The town in modern Uttar Pradesh of which Iltutmish was governor before the Delhi mamluks invited him to take the throne after Aibak’s death in 1210.
Of greater Iran — the Persian-speaking cultural sphere whose architecture, court ceremony and bureaucratic vocabulary the Sultanate inherited through its Ghaznavid and Ghurid predecessors.

2.definition: The eldest surviving son of Iltutmish, an alcoholic widely regarded as politically incompetent. The Turkic nobility put him on the throne in 1236 in defiance of Iltutmish’s will naming Razia; he lasted seven months before Razia deposed him.
Iltutmish’s chief queen and the mother of Razia Sultana. Her royal status was part of the basis on which Iltutmish argued his daughter’s claim over his sons.

A non-Turkic Abyssinian slave-officer whom Razia promoted to master of the royal stables — an enormously influential post. The Turkic nobility took the promotion as an insult; Yakut was killed in the 1240 campaign against Altunia.

The Turkic governor of Bhatinda who revolted against Razia in 1240. He captured her, then married her; the two attempted to retake Delhi together and were defeated and killed near Kaithal in October 1240.

A child sultan of the Mamluk dynasty (ruled 1246–1266) whose real ruler throughout was the regent Ghiyas-ud-din Balban. His long nominal reign was the period in which Balban accumulated the power he would later wield as sultan in his own right.
Balban’s cousin and the frontier governor who held the Multan–Lahore frontier against the Mongols for two decades. Balban had him poisoned in 1270 as part of breaking the Forty’s power.

The rural Muslim-and-Hindu population of Mewat, the region around Delhi, who raided the city’s outskirts in the thirteenth century. Balban campaigned against them as part of his suppression of banditry across the Doab.
Ala ad-Din Muhammad II, the Khwarazmian shah whose empire Genghis Khan destroyed in 1219–21. His son Jalaluddin Mingburnu fled to the Indus, drawing the Mongols to the Sultanate’s frontier.

Of the Himalayas, the high mountain range walling off the northern edge of the Indian subcontinent — here the foothills where the fugitive Khwarazmian prince Jalaluddin disappeared after escaping Genghis Khan at the Indus.

3.definition: The Chagatai Mongol commander whose 1303 invasion reached Delhi and besieged the city — the most dangerous of the six Mongol invasions Alauddin Khalji faced.
A Chagatai Mongol commander who, with Tartaq, led the 1305 invasion that penetrated as far as the modern Saharanpur district before being destroyed by Ulugh Khan.
A Chagatai Mongol commander who, with Ali Beg, led the 1305 invasion of north India that Ulugh Khan’s army systematically destroyed.
A Chagatai Mongol commander whose 1306 invasion reached the lower Punjab — the last of the major Mongol assaults before the Chagatai khanate effectively gave up attacking the Sultanate.
One of Alauddin Khalji’s frontier generals, who broke the army of Qutlugh Khwaja at the Battle of Kili in 1299 — a decisive early defeat of the Mongols outside Delhi.
An Alauddin Khalji general who systematically destroyed the Mongol invasions of 1305 and 1306, sending thousands of prisoners back to Delhi for public execution.
The Chagatai Mongol commander whose army was broken by Zafar Khan at the Battle of Kili outside Delhi in 1299.
The Chahamana (Chauhan) Rajput clan, whose fortress of Ranthambore under Hammir Dev held out against the Sultanate until Alauddin Khalji captured it in 1301 after a year-long siege.

A converted Hindu official and favorite of Mubarak Shah Khalji who murdered him in 1320 and briefly seized the throne before being deposed by Ghazi Malik (Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq), ending the Khalji dynasty.
The small frontier principality founded by Osman I in northwestern Anatolia around 1299 — the seed of the Ottoman Empire, established the same decade Alauddin Khalji was breaking the Mongols.
Of Pakistan, the modern state carved from northwestern British India in 1947, which today claims the Koh-i-Noor alongside India and Afghanistan as a contested colonial-loot trophy.
Of Afghanistan, the mountainous Central Asian country immediately northwest of the Khyber Pass — one of the modern claimants to the Koh-i-Noor, which passed through Afghan hands under the Durranis.

4.definition: A village just outside Delhi where Jauna Khan built a wooden welcome pavilion for his returning father, Sultan Ghiyath al-Din Tughlaq, in 1325. The structure collapsed on the sultan, killing him — an "accident" many suspected was arranged.

The birth name of Muhammad bin Tughlaq before his accession. As Jauna Khan he built the wooden welcome pavilion at Afghanpur that collapsed and killed his father Ghiyas-ud-din in 1325 — possibly an accident, possibly engineered.

The Mongol khanate ruling Persia and the Near East after Hulagu’s conquests; Muhammad bin Tughlaq corresponded with its scholars. Its conversion to Islam under Ghazan Khan in 1295 ended the Mongol-versus-Islam phase of the Eurasian wars.

The ancient Pandya capital deep in the Tamil south, roughly 1,400 miles from Delhi, which Malik Kafur’s 1311 campaign reached — the deepest point of Sultanate military projection into peninsular India.

The autobiography of Firuz Shah Tughlaq, in which he records with pride his suppression of movements he considered unorthodox — Ismaili Shia communities, antinomian Sufi groups, encroaching Hindu temples — and his systematic application of jizya.

One of the short-lived Tughlaq sultans of the post-Firuz Shah succession crisis (1389–1390), none of whom held the throne for more than a few years as the dynasty disintegrated before Timur’s invasion.

A Tughlaq claimant during the chaotic post-Firuz Shah succession, one of the cousins and minor relatives through whom the throne passed as Tughlaq central authority collapsed to Delhi and a few districts.
The last effective Tughlaq sultan, who fielded the army Timur shattered at Loni in December 1398 and fled to Gujarat; the Tughlaq dynasty technically continued for sixteen more years as a fiction.
The converted Hindu official who murdered Mubarak Shah Khalji in 1320 and briefly seized the throne before Ghazi Malik deposed him and founded the Tughlaq dynasty.
Of Morocco, the far-western Islamic land on the Atlantic edge of North Africa — homeland of the great traveler Ibn Battuta, who served Muhammad bin Tughlaq as a judge for eight years.
Followers of Islam — here the Turkic-Persian ruling minority governing a Hindu-majority population, a defining tension of Sultanate rule.

5.definition: The memoir-cum-compilation attributed to Timur, part autobiography and part later Timurid-court compilation, that records his version of the 1398 sack of Delhi and the mass execution of prisoners.
A town in the Punjab whose governorship under the late Sayyid sultans was Bahlul Lodi’s power base before he took Delhi in 1451 and founded the Lodi dynasty.
The town in modern Uttar Pradesh to which the last Sayyid sultan Alam Shah retired as a private gentleman after ceding Delhi to Bahlul Lodi in 1451.

The principal sectarian division of Islam. At the Bahmani court, Persian-speaking Iranian Shia immigrants competed with Sunni Turkic and indigenous Indian Muslim Deccani factions, and the resulting tensions eventually fragmented the empire.
The indigenous Indian Muslim faction at the Bahmani court — locally rooted Deccan Muslims who competed for influence against Persian-speaking Iranian Shia immigrants and Sunni Turkic newcomers.
The site in modern Rajasthan of the March 1527 battle where Babur defeated Rana Sanga’s Rajput coalition, consolidating the Mughal victory at Panipat the year before.

The warrior-clan aristocracy of north-western India — Mewar, Marwar, Amber and others — whose Hindu kingdoms reasserted themselves after Alauddin Khalji’s reductions and resisted Sultanate and later Mughal pressure for centuries.
Of Bengal, the rich rice-growing delta region of eastern India and modern Bangladesh — whose own sultanate patronized a flourishing Bengali-language literature in the fifteenth century.
Shia Muslims from Iran — immigrants who flocked to the Deccan sultanate courts and competed for influence with the local Sunni Turkic and Indian Muslim factions.
Of the Pashtun highlands straddling modern Afghanistan and Pakistan — the warrior background of the Lodi dynasty that would soon take the Delhi throne.

6.definition: The town in modern Uttar Pradesh where the poet Amir Khusrau was born around 1253, the son of a Turkic Lachin officer and a Rajput Hindu mother.
Amir Khusrau’s "Quintet," five long narrative poems modeled on the Persian poet Nizami Ganjavi’s earlier Khamsa — one of the great works of Indo-Persian literature.
Amir Khusrau’s verse chronicle of the rise of the Tughlaq dynasty — one of the principal poetic sources for the dynastic transition from the Khaljis to the Tughlaqs.

Amir Khusrau’s "Nine Heavens," a long poem in praise of India that argues the superiority of Indian intellectual achievements — mathematics, astronomy, music, language — to those of the rest of the Islamic world.

A Persian phrase — "Delhi is still far off" — that Nizamuddin Auliya reportedly uttered when warned the sultan was approaching to compel him to court; the sultan died before reaching Delhi. The phrase became permanent Hindi-Urdu proverbial wisdom for any distant, possibly never-arriving fate.
The converted Hindu official who briefly held the Delhi throne in 1320 after murdering Mubarak Shah Khalji; Amir Khusrau served as court poet under him among seven successive sultans.
Of greater Iran — the Persian-speaking heartland where Sufism took its classical institutional form before spreading east into Sultanate India.
Of the Arabic-speaking Islamic heartland (Arabia, the Levant, Egypt) — the older centers of Sufi practice against which the more Hindu-open Indian Chishti tradition defined itself.
Of Bengal in eastern India — one of the regional vernaculars into which the originally Tamil Bhakti devotional movement spread during the Sultanate period.

7.definition: The last Sharqi sultan of Jaunpur, decisively defeated by Bahlul Lodi in 1486, whose defeat reincorporated Jaunpur’s territory into the Delhi Sultanate after nearly a century of independence.
The pen-name ("Rose-faced") under which Sikandar Lodi wrote Persian verse; he patronized a circle of Persian poets at his Agra court and sponsored translations of Sanskrit texts into Persian.

The dynasty founded by Zafar Khan Muzaffar in 1407 that ruled the wealthy independent Gujarat Sultanate, controlling the Indian Ocean trade through Cambay and Surat until the Mughals annexed it in 1573.
The "Ship Palace" at Mandu, capital of the Malwa Sultanate — a long narrow palace between two lakes, one of the great architectural ensembles of the Sultanate-era Malwa frontier.
A marble-and-sandstone mausoleum at Mandu, capital of the Malwa Sultanate, whose design directly inspired the Taj Mahal a century later.
A congregational mosque in the Bahmani capital of Bidar, part of the distinctive Persian-influenced Indo-Islamic architecture the Bahmani Sultanate produced in the Deccan.
The slave-soldier dynasty that ruled Egypt and Syria from 1250; Selim I’s Ottomans conquered it in 1517, the same era the Lodis ruled Delhi — two ends of the Islamic world in parallel transformation.
The Pashtun Afghan tribe from the Sulaiman mountains to which Bahlul Lodi belonged; the Lodi dynasty was the first non-Turkic, tribally organized dynasty of the Sultanate.

Bahlul Lodi’s political model — treating fellow Pashtun nobles as near-peers sharing decision-making rather than the centralized autocratic Persianate court of Balban or Alauddin. It made the Lodi state more egalitarian within the warrior class but harder to centralize.
The iconic stone shrine in the form of a temple chariot in the Vitthala temple complex at Hampi, the Vijayanagara capital — one of the most photographed monuments of southern India.
A form of the Hindu deity Vishnu/Krishna to whom Krishnadevaraya dedicated the great Vitthala temple at Hampi, famous for its stone chariot and musical pillars.

The Shia dynasty founded in Iran in 1501 by Ismail I, contemporary with the late Lodi Sultanate and the early Mughals; the same gunpowder-versus-cavalry transition that ended the Sultanate at Panipat had already played out against the Safavids at Chaldiran in 1514.

8.definition: Babur’s Turkish gun-master, who had served in the Ottoman army before joining the Timurids and brought the Ottoman wagenburg gunpowder tactics that won the First Battle of Panipat in 1526.
The Afghan city from which Babur ruled as a Timurid prince and launched his invasions of India, capturing Lahore in 1524 before crossing the Indus for the Panipat campaign.

A prominent twentieth-century Indian Marxist historian of the Delhi Sultanate and Mughal economy who, with Mohammad Habib and Romila Thapar, read the Sultanate as a complex multi-ethnic state that prepared the institutional ground for modern Indian state-building.

The working pilgrimage shrine in central Delhi built around the tomb of the Chishti Sufi master Nizamuddin Auliya, with a continuous tradition of Thursday-evening qawwali performance for seven hundred years.
The "Ship Palace" at Mandu, capital of the Malwa Sultanate — a long narrow palace between two lakes, one of the great architectural ensembles of Sultanate-era central India.
The Shia dynasty founded in Iran in 1501; by 1526 the Safavids, the Habsburgs, the Ottomans and the Reformation made up the transformed Eurasian world the Sultanate left behind.

The octagonal double-domed tombs of Sikandar Lodi and Muhammad Shah Sayyid in the modern Lodi Gardens, Delhi — the Lodi dynasty’s principal architectural legacy and the immediate ancestors of Mughal monumental tomb design.
Of Hungary, the central-European kingdom whose army Suleiman the Magnificent shattered at Mohacs in 1526 — the European twin of Babur's gunpowder victory at Panipat the same year.
Of the Pashtun highlands of modern Afghanistan and Pakistan — the homeland of the Lodi dynasty, the last rulers of the Sultanate before Babur.
Followers of Islam — whose geographic distribution across the subcontinent, set during three centuries of Sultanate rule, foreshadowed the religious map of the 1947 Partition.
The Arabian Peninsula — source of the war-horses the Sultanate's perpetually cavalry-short armies imported by sea, and a hub of the Indian Ocean trade network.
Of the Indonesian archipelago (the Spice Islands and Java) — origin of the cloves, nutmeg and pepper that moved through the same Indian Ocean routes the Sultanate's ports tapped.
Of the steppe-and-oasis belt north of Iran (Transoxiana, the Ferghana valley) — the homeland from which both the Sultanate's Turkic founders and its Mughal destroyers under Babur originated.
